title: Slobodan Milošević
subtitle: The Serbian leader who rode nationalism into war

package.intro: In 1987 one sentence to a crowd in Kosovo turned a grey Communist official into the most powerful man in Serbia. Within four years Yugoslavia was at war. This documentary tells how Slobodan Milošević rose on a wave of nationalism, why he became the first sitting head of state charged by an international war crimes tribunal, and why he was never convicted.
facts: Spoke to Serbs at Kosovo Polje on 24 April 1987: 'No one should dare to beat you'
Slovenia and Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991
The Bosnian war (1992–1995) killed about 100,000 people; the Dayton Agreement was signed on 14 December 1995
NATO bombed Yugoslavia for 78 days, 24 March to 10 June 1999
Indicted by the ICTY in May 1999, the first sitting head of state charged by an international war crimes tribunal
Conceded defeat on 6 October 2000 after mass protests in Belgrade
Transferred to The Hague on 28 June 2001; trial began 12 February 2002
Died in custody on 11 March 2006 before a verdict; never convicted
package.sources: International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY case IT-02-54), International Court of Justice (Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro, 2007), Encyclopaedia Britannica, Laura Silber and Allan Little's The Death of Yugoslavia, Adam LeBor's Milosevic: A Biography.

sections.name: Cold open

lines.title: SLOBODAN MILOŠEVIĆ
lines.sub: The Serbian leader who rode nationalism into war

lines: On the twenty-fourth of April 1987, a grey Communist official was sent to calm an angry crowd of Serbs at Kosovo Polje, in Serbia's southern province of Kosovo. Police were pushing them back with batons.

lines.text: No one should dare to beat you!

lines: He stepped out and told them: no one should dare to beat you. The moment was broadcast across Serbia, and it made him a hero almost overnight.

lines.label: estimated deaths in the wars of Yugoslavia's break-up, 1991 – 2001

lines: Within four years, Yugoslavia was at war with itself. The conflicts of the 1990s killed an estimated one hundred and forty thousand people and drove millions from their homes.

lines.text: Charged with war crimes. Never convicted.

lines: Slobodan Milošević became the first sitting head of state to be charged by an international war crimes tribunal. He died before a verdict. This is his story.

sections.name: The apparatchik
lines: Slobodan Milošević was born on the twentieth of August 1941 in Požarevac, a town east of Belgrade, during the German occupation of Yugoslavia.
His family life was marked by tragedy. His father left the family and later took his own life. Years afterwards, so did his mother.

lines.name: Slobodan Milošević
lines.role: Communist official and banker. Rose as Ivan Stambolić's protégé.

lines: At school he met Mirjana Marković, who became his wife and his closest political partner. He studied law in Belgrade and joined the Communist Party.

lines.name: Ivan Stambolić
lines.role: Serbian Communist leader. Milošević's mentor and friend.

lines: His great patron was his friend Ivan Stambolić, a rising Communist leader. Stambolić helped him run a state gas company, and then one of Belgrade's biggest banks.

Yugoslavia, rebuilt after the Second World War by the Communist leader Tito, was a federation of six republics. After Tito died in 1980, it was held together by a weak collective leadership and a failing economy.

sections.name: The rise

lines.place: Eighth Session · League of Communists of Serbia

lines: Stambolić had helped make him head of Serbia's Communist party. In 1987, months after the speech at Kosovo Polje, Milošević turned on his mentor and forced him out.
Then came huge rallies, which his supporters called the anti-bureaucratic revolution. Crowds brought down the leaders of Vojvodina, Kosovo and Montenegro, and his allies replaced them.
In 1989, Kosovo's autonomy was cut back. Its Albanian majority lost control of its own police and courts, and in the years that followed, many Albanians were dismissed from state jobs.

lines.text: They are not armed battles, although such things cannot yet be excluded.

lines: In June 1989, on the six hundredth anniversary of a medieval battle against the Ottomans, he told a vast crowd in Kosovo that Serbs again faced battles. They are not armed battles, he said, although such things cannot yet be excluded.

sections.name: The wars
lines: In 1990, elections brought nationalist leaders to power in other republics too, including Franjo Tuđman in Croatia. On the twenty-fifth of June 1991, Slovenia and Croatia declared independence.
Serbs in Croatia, fearful of the new Croatian state, rebelled. They were backed by the Yugoslav army, increasingly under Belgrade's control, and large parts of Croatia were seized.
The town of Vukovar was besieged for three months and reduced to ruins. After it fell, around two hundred prisoners taken from its hospital were murdered at a nearby farm.

In 1992 the war spread to Bosnia. Bosnian Serb forces led by Radovan Karadžić and General Ratko Mladić besieged Sarajevo, and drove Bosniaks and Croats out of large areas in what became known as ethnic cleansing.
Prison camps were set up in northern Bosnia. When journalists filmed starving prisoners behind wire in the summer of 1992, the pictures shocked the world.
Milošević insisted Serbia was not at war. Prosecutors later argued that Belgrade armed, paid and directed the Bosnian Serb army and paramilitary groups such as Arkan's Tigers.
In July 1995, Mladić's forces overran the UN safe area of Srebrenica and killed more than eight thousand Bosniak men and boys. International courts have ruled that it was genocide.

lines.label: estimated monthly inflation in Yugoslavia, January 1994

lines: At home, UN sanctions and war spending wrecked the economy. In January 1994, prices were rising by an estimated three hundred million percent a month, one of the worst bouts of hyperinflation ever recorded.

sections.name: The peacemaker
lines: In 1995 the tide turned. Croatia's army retook most of its lost territory, and around two hundred thousand Serbs fled or were driven out. NATO bombed Bosnian Serb positions.
Milošević now presented himself as a peacemaker. At talks on an American air base in Dayton, Ohio, he negotiated on behalf of the Bosnian Serbs.
The Dayton Agreement ended the Bosnian war. About one hundred thousand people had been killed in Bosnia alone, and more than two million had fled their homes.

At home, his government tried to overturn opposition wins in local elections in 1996. Months of street protests forced him to back down. In 1997 he became president of what remained of Yugoslavia: Serbia and Montenegro.

sections.name: Kosovo
lines: In 1998, fighting broke out in Kosovo between an Albanian guerrilla army and Serbian forces. In January 1999, forty-five Albanians were killed in the village of Račak.

When peace talks failed, NATO began bombing Yugoslavia in March 1999, without the approval of the UN Security Council. The campaign lasted seventy-eight days, and hundreds of civilians were killed by the bombing.
On the ground, Serbian forces drove out Kosovo's Albanians. Around eight hundred and fifty thousand people fled or were expelled, and thousands of civilians were killed.
In May 1999, the UN war crimes tribunal for the former Yugoslavia charged him with crimes against humanity in Kosovo. In June, he agreed to pull his forces out.

sections.name: The fall
lines: In August 2000, his old mentor Ivan Stambolić, by then a critic, vanished while out jogging in Belgrade. His remains were found in 2003, and members of a state security unit were later convicted of his murder.
That September, Milošević lost a presidential election to the opposition candidate, Vojislav Koštunica, and tried to force a second round.
On the fifth of October, hundreds of thousands of people poured into Belgrade. Protesters stormed the parliament, part of it caught fire, and the police stood aside. The next day, he conceded.
In April 2001 he was arrested at his villa after a standoff. That June, Serbia's prime minister, Zoran Đinđić, had him handed over to the tribunal in The Hague.

sections.name: The trial
lines: His trial opened in February 2002. He faced sixty-six counts covering Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo, including genocide in Bosnia.

lines.name: The defendant
lines.role: Defended himself and called the tribunal illegal. Faced 66 counts.

lines: He refused a lawyer, defended himself, and called the court illegitimate. Many Serbs watched on television and agreed with him.
The trial dragged on for four years. On the eleventh of March 2006, with a verdict still months away, he was found dead in his cell. He had suffered a heart attack.
Because he died, he was never convicted of anything. The case against him was never tested by a final judgment.

sections.name: Legacy
lines: Tens of thousands of supporters attended a farewell rally in Belgrade. He was buried under a tree in the garden of his family home in Požarevac.

Other courts did reach verdicts. Karadžić and Mladić were convicted of genocide and sentenced to life. In 2007, the International Court of Justice ruled that Serbia had failed to prevent the genocide at Srebrenica.
In Serbia, opinion is still divided. Some see him as a leader who stood up for Serbs as Yugoslavia collapsed, and point out that all sides committed crimes.
Most historians see him as the politician who did more than anyone to turn those fears into war.
Milošević did not create the old fears of the Balkans. He discovered, in a crowd at Kosovo Polje, that they could carry him to power. The price was paid by others.
